Amylase is an enzyme that breaks down starch. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Amylase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2006_2)
Phospholipase A2 (PLA2) participates in a wide range of cellular processes including inflammation and transmembrane signaling.
The 3D structure includes two copies of the enzyme bound to DNA.
This historic PDB entry is the first atomic structure of an enzyme. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Lysozyme](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2000_9)

Pepsin is a digestive enzyme that cleaves proteins in our food. This structure shows the active enzyme. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Pepsin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2000_12)

In digestion, trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase work together to chop up proteins. Pancreatic cells make an inhibitor that blocks the action of trypsin. The 3D structure includes the inhibitor bound in the active site of the enzyme. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Trypsin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2003_10)

Carboxypeptidase belongs to the first structures solved by x-ray crystallography and served as an early model for protein-cutting enzymes. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Carboxypeptidase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2011_10)
The 3D structure has phosphate bound in the active site. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Ribonuclease](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2008_9)
Biological molecules perform their tasks in an environment surrounded by water.
Glucose is a simple sugar molecule that is broken down in cells to generate chemical energy.
ATP is used to transfer chemical energy between different biological molecules.

Serum albumin transports insoluble carbon-rich molecules like fatty acids in the blood. This structure includes the protein bound to several fatty acid molecules. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Serum Albumin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2003_1)

PDB entry [1m1j](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1m1j) includes the main portion of the molecule, and PDB entry [2baf](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/2BAF) includes a flexible portion of one chain. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Fibrin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2006_11)

Thrombin is a protein-cutting protein that activates the proteins that form blood clots. This structure includes the active form of thrombin. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Thrombin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2002_1)

Two 3D structures are included here: [1xka](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1xka) includes the protein-cutting portion involved in signaling, and [1iod](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1iod) binds to membranes using calcium ions. The structure in 1iod also includes a snake venom protein.
Insulin is a hormone that controls glucose levels in the blood. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Insulin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_2)
EGF is a hormone that helps regulate cell growth. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Epidermal Growth Factor](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2010_6)
Glucagon is a hormone that raises the glucose levels in the bloodstream, counteracting the effect of insulin.

Antibodies recognize foreign molecules in the blood as part of the immune system that protects us from infection. This structure includes an entire antibody. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Antibody](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_9)

Rhinovirus is composed of a short RNA genome surrounded by a symmetrical protein capsid. This structure includes coordinates for the capsid. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Rhinovirus](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_8)

Cytochrome c is a small protein that transports electrons during the process of energy production. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Cytochrome c](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2002_12)

Complex IV, also known as cytochrome c oxidase, performs the last step of the respiratory electron transport chain. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Cytochrome c Oxidase (Complex IV)](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2000_5)

Complex III, also known as cytochrome bc1, transfers protons across the mitochondrial membrane as part of the respiratory electron transport chain. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Cytochrome bc1 (Complex III)](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2011_5)

Succinate dehydrogenase performs the sixth step of the citric acid cycle, removing hydrogen atoms and transferring them to ubiquinone, for use in the electron transport chain. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Succinate Dehydrogenase (Complex II)](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2012_10)

Complex I, also known as NADH:quinone oxidoreductase, performs the first step in respiratory electron transport. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [NADH-Quinone Oxidoreductase (Complex I)](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2011_12)

ATP synthase is one of the wonders of the molecular world. ATP synthase is an enzyme, a molecular motor, an ion pump, and another molecular motor all wrapped together in one amazing nanoscale machine. It plays an indispensable role in our cells, building most of the ATP that powers our cellular processes. The mechanism by which it performs this task is a real surprise.. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [ATP Synthase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2005_12)

Cyclooxygenase performs the first step in the creation of pain-signaling prostaglandins by adding two oxygen molecules to arachidonic acid. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Cyclooxygenase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_5)

The calcium pump transports calcium ions across cell membranes. This structure includes the conformation with calcium halfway through the membrane. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Calcium Pump](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_3)
Potassium channels allow potassium ions to pass through the membrane. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Potassium Channel](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2003_2)

P-glycoprotein pumps drugs and other toxic molecules out of our cells, powered by ATP. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [P-glycoprotein](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2010_3)

Rhodopsin senses light in the retina. This structure includes rhodopsin before it has absorbed light, with the cofactor retinal in the bent, cis conformation. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Rhodopsin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2012_3)

EGF is a message telling cells that they have permission to grow. It is released by cells in areas of active growth, then is either picked up by the cell itself or by neighboring cells, stimulating their ability to divide. The message is received by a receptor on the cell surface, which binds to EGF and relays the message to signaling proteins inside the cell, ultimately mobilizing the processes needed for growth.PDB ID: [1ivo](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1ivo), [2jwa](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/2jwa), [2gs6](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/2gs6). Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2010_6)

The Ras protein, shown here from PDB entry [5p21](http://www.rcsb.org/pdb/explore/explore.do?structureId=5p21) , uses this approach. It is normally in the "off" state, with GDP bound in the site. To turn it "on," the GDP is swapped for GTP. Then, after the signal is delivered, the GTP is cleaved to GDP and phosphate, turning the protein firmly off. It is particularly important that Ras has an unambiguous off state, because it is intimately involved in the control of cell growth. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Ras Protein](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2012_4)

Acetylcholine receptor binds to the neurotransmitter acetylcholine and opens a channel, as part of the process of signaling across nerve synapses. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Acetylcholine Receptor](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2005_11)

Adrenergic receptors bind to the hormone adrenaline and activate signaling proteins inside the cell. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Beta2-Adrenergic Receptor/Gs Protein](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2008_4)

Photosynthetic reaction centers capture individual light photons and use them to provide power for building sugar. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Photosystem II](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_11)

Light-harvesting complex is used by plants and photosynthetic bacteria to absorb more of light than would be captured by the photosynthetic reaction center alone. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Light-harvesting Complex](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_11)

Some bacteria used a smaller photosynthetic reaction center to capture light. This structure includes one from a purple bacterium. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Photosynthetic Reaction Center](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_10)
Hemoglobin transports oxygen in the blood. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Hemoglobin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2003_5)
Myoglobin stores oxygen in cells and is particularly plentiful in muscle cells. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Myoglobin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2000_1)
Ferritin forms a hollow shell that stores iron. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Ferritin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2002_11)
Thymidylate synthase is an enzyme that creates thymine nucleotides for use in building DNA.
Tryptophan synthase is an enzyme the performs the last two steps in the synthesis of the amino acid tryptophan.

Glutamine synthetase is a large allosteric enzyme that connects ammonia and glutamate to form glutamine. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Glutamine Synthetase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2002_6)
Leucine aminopeptidase is a protein-digesting enzyme that cuts leucine amino acids from the end of a protein.

Fatty acid synthase contains several enzymes that together synthesize fatty acids. This structure includes the multienzyme complex from fungal cells. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Fatty Acid Synthase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2007_6)

Nitrogenase is used by nitrogen-fixing bacteria to convert inert nitrogen gas into biologically-useful ammonia. This structure includes the entire nitrogenase enzyme, including the central MoFe protein that performs the reaction, and the outer Fe protein that powers the reaction. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Nitrogenase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2002_2)

Dihydrofolate reductase is an enzyme that activates a carbon-carrying cofactor in biosynthetic reactions. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Dihydrofolate Reductase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2002_10)
Aspartate carbamoyltransferase is an enzyme that performs the first step in the synthesis of nucleotide bases like thymine and cytosine.
Catalase detoxifies hydrogen peroxide in cells. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Catalase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_9)

Bacteria protect themselves by building enzymes that break down antibiotics. This structure shows one of the enzymes that break down drugs like penicillin. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [beta-Lactamase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2002_5)
In animal cells, Alcohol dehydrogenase detoxifies ethanol. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Alcohol Dehydrogenase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_1)
Hexokinase performs the first step in glycolysis, using an ATP molecule to start the process. It transfers a phosphate from ATP to glucose, forming glucose-6-phosphate.
Phosphoglucose isomerase performs the second reaction of glycolysis. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Phosphoglucose Isomerase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_2)

Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase performs the sixth step of glycolysis. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate Dehydrogenase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_2)
Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate aldolase performs the fourth step of glycolysis. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Aldolase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_2)

Phosphofructokinase performs the third step of glycolysis. It is an allosteric enzyme that regulates the pathway. This structure is the active form. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Phosphofructokinase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_2)
Triose phosphate isomerase performs the fifth step of glycolysis. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Triosephosphate Isomerase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_2)
Actin forms filaments that are important for cell structure and mobility. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month articles: [Actin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_7)
Phosphoglycerate mutase performs the eighth step of glycolysis. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Phospoglycerate Mutase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_2)

Phosphoglycerate kinase performs the seventh step of glycolysis. This structure is the open form of the enzyme, before substrates bind. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Phosphoglycerate Kinase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_2)
Enolase performs the ninth step of glycolysis. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Enolase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_2)

Pyruvate kinase performs the last step of glycolysis. It is an allosteric enzyme that regulates the pathway. This structure is the active form. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Pyruvate Kinase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_2)

GFP is a fluorescent protein from jellyfish, now widely used in biotechnology. This structure includes the protein and its fluorescent chromophore. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Green Fluorescent Protein](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2003_6)

Luciferase is an enzyme that creates light. This structure includes the enzyme from fireflies, along with the luciferin cofactor that is important in the light-producing reaction. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Luciferase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2006_6)

RuBisCo performs the reaction that captures carbon dioxide and uses it to build sugar molecules. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [RuBisCo: Ribulose Bisphosphate Carboxylase/Oxygenase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2000_11)

Microtubules are huge, sturdy filaments that extend through the cytoplasm, providing support and providing tracks for the motion of two types of protein motors: kinesin and dynein. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Microtubule](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2014_7)

Actin forms filaments that are important for cell structure and mobility. Myosin is the molecular motor that powers the muscle contraction. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month articles: [Actin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_7), [Myosin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_6)

Proteasomes are the cell's protein recyclers. Proteins need to be destroyed for many reasons: they may be damaged, or they may be part of an invading virus, or they simply may not be needed any more. Proteasomes provide a controlled method for breaking down proteins safely within the environment of the cell. They chop obsolete or damaged proteins into small pieces, about 2 to 25 amino acids in length. Most of these are then completely broken down into amino acids by peptidases in the cell. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article Proteasome

A chain of ubiquitin molecules are added to obsolete proteins, indicating that they need to be destroyed. This structure includes a single ubiquitin molecule. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Ubiquitin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2004_12)

HSP90 is a chaperone that assists the folding of immature proteins. This structure includes HSP90 in the closed, active form and the helper protein Sba1. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Heat Shock Protein Hsp90](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2008_12)

EF-Ts charges EF-Tu with GTP, making it ready to deliver a new tRNA to the ribosome. This structure includes the complex of EF-Ts with EF-Tu. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Elongation Factor Ts and Tu](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2006_9)
Proline cis/trans isomerase is an enzyme that flips the conformation of proline amino acids in protein chains, helping them fold in the proper way.

Protein chaperones guide the proper folding of new proteins. This bacterial chaperone has a hollow chamber inside that protects proteins as they fold. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Chaperonin GroEL/ES](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2002_8)

Prefoldin protects proteins while they are folding into their proper shape. It is shaped like a jellyfish, with arms that surround the folding protein. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Prefoldin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2002_8)

EF-G ejects a spent tRNA from the ribosome after its amino acid has been added to the growing chain, and then pushes the messenger RNA forward by one codon. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Elongation Factor G](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2006_9)

Ribosomes are the molecule machines that build new proteins based on the genetic information carried in messenger RNA. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Ribosome](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2010_1)

EF-Tu delivers charged tRNA to the ribosome during protein synthesis. This structure includes EF-Tu and a phenylalanyl-tRNA. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Elongation Factor Tu/tRNA](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2006_9)

Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases add the proper amino acid to the many different forms of transfer RNA. This structure includes the enzyme that adds asparate to its tRNA. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Aspartyl-tRNA Synthetase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_4)

Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases add the proper amino acid to the many different forms of transfer RNA. This structure includes the enzyme that adds phenylalanine to its tRNA. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Phenylalanyl-tRNA Synthetase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_4)

Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases add the proper amino acid to the many different forms of transfer RNA. This structure includes the enzyme that adds phenylalanine to its tRNA. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Threonyl-tRNA Synthetase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_4)

Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases add the proper amino acid to the many different forms of transfer RNA. This structure includes the enzyme that adds phenylalanine to its tRNA. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Isoleucyl-tRNA Synthetase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_4)

Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases add the proper amino acid to the many different forms of transfer RNA. This structure includes the enzyme that adds phenylalanine to its tRNA. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Valyl-tRNA Synthetase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_4)

Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases add the proper amino acid to the many different forms of transfer RNA. This structure includes the enzyme that adds phenylalanine to its tRNA. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Glutaminyl-tRNA Synthetase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_4)

Transfer RNA is used during the synthesis of proteins to match a three-nucleotide codon in messenger RNA with the proper amino acid that will be added to the protein. This historic structure was the first structure of a tRNA, solved in the laboratory of Aaron Klug. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Transfer RNA](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_3)
Myosin is the molecular motor that powers the muscle contraction. [Myosin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_6)
Myosin is the molecular motor that powers the muscle contraction. [Myosin](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_6)

DNA encodes genetic information in a chain of nucleotides. This historical structure was the first atomic structure of B-form DNA, and includes a short DNA double helix twelve nucleotides long. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [DNA](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2001_11)

Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific nucleotide sequences, and are widely used in biotechnology. This structure shows EcoRI, a restriction enzyme from Escherichia coli, with a small piece of DNA bound in the active site. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Restriction Endonuclease EcoRI](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2000_8)

Ultraviolet light can form crosslinks between adjacent bases in DNA, leading to mutations when the DNA is replicated. This structure includes an enzyme that recognizes thymine dimers and breaks the crosslink. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [DNA Photolyase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2007_7)

Class I topoisomerases bind to DNA and release tension caused by winding or unwinding of the double helix. This structure includes the enzyme and a short piece of DNA captured before the cleavage reaction that relaxes the DNA. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Topoisomerase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2006_1)

RNA polymerase transcribes the genetic information in DNA, creating a complementary strand of RNA. This structure includes the enzyme along with short pieces of DNA and RNA, showing the process of transcription. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [RNA Polymerase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2003_4)

CAP is activated by cyclic AMP and then stimulates the synthesis of enzymes that break down food. This structure includes the protein and a short piece of DNA, which is sharply bent by the protein. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Catabolite Gene Activator Protein](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2003_12)

The lac repressor binds to the lac operon, controlling the production of enzymes that are involved in lactose metabolism. It is composed of identical chains that fold into several functional domains. This structure includes the domain that senses the level of lactose and the domains that bind to DNA. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [lac Repressor](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2003_3)

This complex of proteins binds to DNA in front of the start site for transcription, helping to melt the DNA and get RNA polymerase started. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [TATA-binding Protein/ Transcription Factor IIB](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2005_7)

DNA helicase separates the two strands in a DNA double helix, powered by ATP. This structure includes the bacterial DNA helicase DnaB bound to single-stranded DNA. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [DNA Helicase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2013_12)

Taq polymerase is a DNA polymerase from the Thermus aquaticus. It is often used in biotechnology because it is particularly stable at high temperatures. The structure includes a small piece of DNA in the polymerase active site. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [DNA Polymerase](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2000_3)
Single-stranded DNA-binding proteins protect DNA during replication, when it is not wound into a double helix.
This protein packages DNA in bacterial cells.

DNA is packaged inside the nucleus in nucleosomes. This structure shows a long piece of DNA wrapped around histone proteins to form a nucleosome. Learn more from the Molecule of the Month article [Nucleosome](http://dx.doi.org/10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2000_7)
